title: Image Converter
dek: PNG, JPG, WebP, BMP, GIF — in one side, any of them out the other. Batch as many as you like.
meta: Convert images between PNG, JPG, WebP, BMP and more, in batch and entirely in your browser. Free, no uploads, no watermarks.

steps.p: Any mix of formats. The list shows a thumbnail per file.
JPG, PNG, WebP or BMP, with a quality slider for the lossy formats. Optional max-width for shrinking on the way out.
Everything converts at once; the ZIP button gathers the lot.

faq.q: Are the conversions done online?
faq.a: No — your browser has a full image engine built in, and that's what's used. The files never touch a server because there isn't one.

faq.q: Why did my PNG turn white around the edges?
faq.a: JPG has no transparency. If a transparent PNG goes to JPG, the background has to become something — white is the default. Output to PNG or WebP to keep transparency.

title: Compress Images
dek: Cut image weight for faster pages and lighter emails. Quality slider plus optional size cap — no mystery settings.
meta: Compress JPG and PNG images with a quality slider and optional max width. See before/after sizes, keep files private. No uploads.

steps.p: Original sizes are listed as they load.
80 looks like 100 to nearly everyone. 60 starts to show on close inspection. Optionally cap the longest side to shrink further.
Each result shows exactly how much smaller it got.

faq.q: How much smaller will my files get?
faq.a: Photos typically drop 50–80% at quality 80. Flat graphics and screenshots compress less — they were already efficient — so try WebP output for those.

faq.q: Does compressing lose quality?
faq.a: At 80+, essentially never perceptibly. Below 60 you're trading visible quality for size — the preview will show you before you commit.

title: Resize Images
dek: Exact pixels or a percentage — set the width, height, or both, and keep the aspect ratio if you want it kept.
meta: Resize images to exact pixel dimensions or percentages with high-quality scaling. Batch resize in your browser. Free, private, offline.

steps.p: The dimensions appear next to each file.
Type a width, a height, or a percentage. With 'keep ratio' on, giving one side fills the other automatically.
Everything resizes consistently, ready to download.

faq.q: How is the quality after an upscale?
faq.a: Scaling up can't invent detail that wasn't there. It won't blur like a phone screenshot — Lanczos-quality resampling is used — but 2x is the practical limit.

faq.q: Can I resize by exact percentage?
faq.a: Yes — switch to percent mode and set 50% to halve every dimension, handy for @2x assets.

title: Crop Images
dek: Drag a box over the part you want, check the preview, done. Several images at once uses the same box on each.
meta: Crop images visually — drag a selection, fine-tune the numbers, export cleanly. Runs fully in your browser, nothing uploaded.

steps.p: It opens in the cutter with a live selection box.
Move the box, or type exact pixel coordinates on the right. The preview updates as you go.
The cropped image downloads as PNG or JPG.

faq.q: Can I crop a batch with the same rectangle?
faq.a: Yes — add more images and the same pixel box applies to each. Useful for screenshots of the same app or scans.

faq.q: What's the smallest crop I can make?
faq.a: No practical minimum; if you can drag it, you can crop it.

title: Rotate Images
dek: Quarter turns, half turns, or any angle in between — with the corners filled so nothing goes missing.
meta: Rotate images by 90°, 180°, 270° or a custom angle with automatic canvas fitting. In-browser, free, no uploads.

steps.p: Single or batch.
Quick buttons for the two right turns and the half turn, or type any angle — 3° of straightening on a crooked photo, say.
Batch results arrive zipped or individually.

faq.q: Does a custom angle crop the corners?
faq.a: No — the canvas grows to fit the rotated image, so nothing is cut off. The new file's dimensions adjust accordingly.

faq.q: Does rotating lose quality?
faq.a: Right-angle turns are mathematically lossless. Free angles resample once, which at normal quality settings is invisible.

title: Flip Images
dek: Mirror any image horizontally or vertically — fixing selfies, reversing scans, making not-so-subtle design jokes.
meta: Flip images horizontally or vertically in your browser. Free, instant, no uploads, no quality loss.

steps.p: Previews show what you're about to mirror.
Horizontal is the mirror look; vertical is the ink-blot look. Both at once is a 180° turn.
Done — pixels rearranged, nothing re-compressed unnecessarily.

faq.q: Is flipping different from rotating?
faq.a: Yes — a flip mirrors the image, so left and right swap. A 180° rotation is a flip both ways, which is why they can look similar at a glance.

faq.q: Does it affect quality?
faq.a: The rearrangement itself is lossless; only the export format's compression touches the pixels.

title: Watermark Images
dek: Put your mark on photos: text or logo, any corner, opacity you control. Batch it — every image gets the same stamp.
meta: Add text or logo watermarks to one image or a whole batch — position, size and opacity control included. Offline, private.

steps.p: Batch works — one watermark setting applies to all.
Text with custom colour and background pill, or a logo image with opacity control. Place it in any corner.
The live preview shows the result before you commit.

faq.q: Can I use a transparent PNG logo?
faq.a: Yes — transparency is respected. Scale it down as a percentage of the photo so it fits consistently.

faq.q: Can the watermark be tiled across the whole image?
faq.a: Single placement for now, corner or centre. Tiling gets busy fast and adds options nobody uses twice.

title: Favicon Generator
dek: One image in — a proper favicon.ico, PNG set and the HTML snippet to paste into your site's head.
meta: Generate favicon.ico and the full PNG icon set (16–512px) from a single image, plus copy-paste HTML. Free, browser-based.

steps.p: At least 512×512 is ideal. Non-square images are centred and fitted.
See exactly how 16×16 in a browser tab will look — the honest test.
favicon.ico with every useful size packed inside, the PNG set, and a snippet for your <head>.

faq.q: What sizes go inside the .ico?
faq.a: 16, 32 and 48 pixels — the set browsers actually use. The PNG set adds 180 (Apple) and 192/512 (Android) for completeness.

faq.q: Where do I put these files?
faq.a: Site root, next to index.html, then paste the snippet into your <head>. That's the whole ritual.

title: SVG to PNG
dek: Rasterise vector files at any size you like — 16px icons or 4000px posters from the same SVG.
meta: Convert SVG vector files to PNG at custom pixel sizes with transparent backgrounds. In your browser, no uploads, no dependencies.

steps.p: The natural dimensions are read and shown.
Paste a target width, or a multiplier: 2×, 4× for retina- and poster-sized exports.
PNG by default; JPG and WebP available where you don't need transparency.

faq.q: My SVG converted to a blank image — why?
faq.a: SVGs that reference external images or fonts can't load them in the sandbox. Flatten those first (most editors can).

faq.q: Can I export with a background colour?
faq.a: Yes — pick a background colour in the options, or leave it transparent.

title: HEIC to JPG
h1: Convert HEIC to JPG or PNG
dek: The photos your iPhone insists on — converted to formats everything else in the world opens.
meta: Convert iPhone HEIC/HEIF photos to JPG or PNG in your browser. Batch friendly, free, private — no uploads, no limits.

steps.p: Straight off an iPhone, or a batch from Photos. Multiple files welcome.
JPG is the safe universal choice; PNG if you'll edit the result.
If there was motion or depth data, it's skipped — the still image is what gets converted.

faq.q: Why bother converting?
faq.a: Windows tools, older editors and half the web treat HEIC like a foreign language. JPG opens everywhere, instantly.

faq.q: Why is this conversion slower than the others?
faq.a: HEIC decode is heavy, real work — a few seconds per photo rather than a blink. Worth it for not uploading your camera roll anywhere.

title: TIFF to PNG
h1: Convert TIFF to PNG or JPG
dek: Scanners love TIFF. Browsers don't. Bridge the gap without installing anything.
meta: Convert TIFF files to PNG or JPG in your browser — including multi-page TIFFs, saved page by page. Free, private, no uploads.

steps.p: Single or multi-page; each page becomes its own image.
PNG keeps every pixel; JPG keeps your disk happy.
Multi-page archives arrive zipped.

faq.q: What kind of TIFFs are supported?
faq.a: The common ones from scanners and photo tools. Exotic colour spaces may come out oddly — if so, tell the tool (contact page) and it can be looked at.

faq.q: Can I keep it as TIFF?
faq.a: The point is to escape TIFF, but if you need TIFF output, any image editor will re-save it from the PNG.

title: Image to Base64
dek: Data-URI output with copy-ready snippets for HTML, CSS and Markdown — for when you want the image inline.
meta: Convert any image to a Base64 data URI, with ready-made HTML, CSS and Markdown snippets. Browser-only, instant, no uploads.

steps.p: Keep it small — data URIs live inside your code, so every byte is paid for twice.
Raw Base64, an HTML img tag, a CSS background, or Markdown.
No files to keep. That's the point and the trade.

faq.q: When is Base64 a good idea?
faq.a: Tiny icons and UI bullets that save a request. Not photos — the same bytes inflated by a third, in a file you can't cache separately.

faq.q: Is anything sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The conversion is base arithmetic the browser does locally.

title: Base64 to Image
h1: Convert Base64 back to an image
dek: Pasted data URI or raw Base64 — decoded into a real image file you can save.
meta: Decode Base64 or data-URI strings back into PNG, JPG or WebP image files. See the preview before you save. No uploads, free.

steps.p: With or without the data:image/... header — the tool works either way.
If it's valid, you'll see the image. If not, you'll see exactly what's wrong with the input.
The original format is detected from the data itself.

faq.q: It says the Base64 is invalid. Now what?
faq.a: Usual suspects: the string is truncated, wrapped in quotes, or has stray whitespace mid-string. Everything after 'base64,' is the part that matters.

faq.q: Can it decode huge strings?
faq.a: Yes, within browser memory — several MB of Base64 is routine.

title: EXIF Viewer
dek: See what your camera wrote into the file: the camera, settings, dates — and the GPS coordinates, which surprise most people.
meta: View EXIF metadata in JPG photos — camera, settings, timestamps, and GPS location. Read privately in your browser. No uploads.

steps.p: JPG and HEIC-JPG photos carry the most metadata.
Camera and exposure, date and time, GPS coordinates (with a map link if present), plus the full tag table.
Sharing the photo with the location attached was probably not the plan. The EXIF remover handles that.

faq.q: What's the GPS thing about?
faq.a: Most phones embed the exact location in every photo by default. Post that picture of your home and you've posted your home's coordinates.

faq.q: No metadata shown — why?
faq.a: The photo was already stripped (social apps remove it), or it's a format that doesn't carry EXIF, like plain PNG.

title: Remove EXIF Data
dek: One click between a photo and the internet. Removes camera details, timestamps and GPS location — pixels untouched.
meta: Remove EXIF and GPS metadata from JPG photos before sharing them. Batch friendly, browser-based, free. Your photos stay yours.

steps.p: Batch works — holiday albums welcome.
The EXIF viewer shows exactly what's about to be removed, if you're curious.
Fresh files with no EXIF. They look exactly the same — only the hidden metadata goes away.

faq.q: Does stripping change how the photo looks?
faq.a: No. Orientation is baked in correctly before removal, so the photo won't suddenly rotate weirdly in other apps.

faq.q: Should I remove metadata from every photo?
faq.a: Any photo headed for a public place — marketplaces, forums, social media after they've re-compressed it — is safer stripped. Your own archive copy can keep everything.
